newsitem.title: FRANCE: French banks kept assets of deported Jews - paper.
newsitem.headline: French banks kept assets of deported Jews - paper.

text.p: French banks, like their Swiss counterparts, kept funds deposited by Jews killed in Nazi death camps in World War Two and later failed to turn the money over to a government agency as ordered, the newspaper Le Monde said on Saturday.
Le Monde said experts estimated the money at today's equivalent of at least one billion francs ($135 million).
But the newspaper, which devoted a full page to its investigation of the issue, said it concluded bureaucracy and confusion, rather than any specific policy, were to blame.
Some 76,000 Jews, a quarter of those in France, were deported to camps during the 1940-1944 German occupation and only about 2,000 survived.
German military orders froze all Jewish accounts in 1941 and banks continued after the war to automatically destroy records about accounts which had not been used for over 10 years, Le Monde said.
A 1966 law, reinforced in 1977, ordered banks to turn over funds and records from such accounts to a special government agency but hardly any actually did, Le Monde wrote.

The banking association (AFB) told Le Monde its members broke no laws. It said it would seek to track accounts now but one bank said that its paper archives, if put back-to-back would extend 90 km (54 miles).

Prime Minister Alain Juppe promised French Jewish leaders this year that an investigatory body would seek to establish what became of funds and property confiscated by the Nazis or by the collaborationist Vichy regime.
Most interest has revolved around some 2,000 works of art, from some 65,000 seized by the Nazis, and which were not claimed by their owners after the war.
But most Jews deported from France were largely penniless recent immigrants from east and central Europe and Jewish leaders say the issue is one of moral recognition rather than restitution of funds.
Switzerland, which was neutral during the war, has been under heavy criticism in recent months after revelations that its banks dealt with the Nazis.
